claim: Animals can effortlessly adapt their behavior by generalizing from past aversive experiences, allowing to avoid harm in novel situations.
source: Animals can effortlessly adapt their behavior by generalizing from past aversive experiences, allowing to avoid harm in novel situations.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal behavior that draws from established scientific understanding of fear generalization and adaptive behavior.

claim: Aversive learning changed scanning patterns selectively along the adversity-related dimension, but not the orthogonal dimension.
source: Aversive learning changed scanning patterns selectively along the adversity-related dimension, but not the orthogonal dimension.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the FPSA analysis and statistical comparisons presented in the results section.

claim: The effect of changed scanning patterns was mainly located within the eye region of faces.
source: This effect was mainly located within the eye region of faces.
evidence: This is supported by the searchlight FPSA analysis and ROI-based comparisons showing significant effects in the eye region.

claim: Fear generalization makes it possible to promptly deploy defensive behavior when similar situations are encountered anew.
source: While fear generalization makes it possible to promptly deploy defensive behavior when similar situations are encountered anew (Guttman and Kalish, 1956; Hovland, 1937; Pavlov, 1927; Shepard, 1987; Spence, 1937; Struyf et al., 2015; Tenenbaum and Griffiths, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on fear generalization.

claim: Selectivity ensures that only truly aversive stimuli are recognized as aversive, thus avoiding costly false alarms.
source: selectivity ensures that only truly aversive stimuli are recognized as aversive (Li et al., 2008; Onat and Büchel, 2015), thus avoiding costly false alarms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on stimulus selectivity in aversive learning.

claim: Eye-movements can rapidly determine what information is available in a scene for recognizing adversity.
source: A central part of active exploration are eye-movements which can rapidly determine what information is available in a scene for recognizing adversity (Dowd et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on eye-movements and scene exploration.

claim: Humans explore complex stimuli serially.
source: Humans explore such complex stimuli serially (Itti and Koch, 2001; Onat et al., 2014; Parkhurst et al., 2002; Tatler et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on visual exploration.

claim: Humans rely heavily on their overt attentional resources due to well documented perceptual bottleneck for forming detailed representations of complex scenes.
source: rely heavily on their overt attentional resources due to well documented perceptual bottleneck for forming detailed representations of complex scenes (Ahissar and Hochstein, 2004; Hochstein and Ahissar, 2002; Treisman and Gelade, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on attention and perception.

claim: Active viewing of faces is a key ability during daily social interactions.
source: First, active viewing of faces is a key ability during daily social interactions (Cerf et al., 2009; End and Gamer, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on face viewing in social contexts.

claim: Detecting minute differences in the configuration of facial elements is crucial for inferring the identity or emotional content of a face.
source: where detecting minute differences in the configuration of facial elements is crucial for inferring the identity or emotional content of a face (Adolphs, 2008; Jack et al., 2014; Peterson and Eckstein, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on face perception.

claim: The universal spatial configuration of facial elements makes it easily possible to generate faces with subtle differences that globally form a perceptual similarity continuum.
source: Second, the universal spatial configuration of facial elements makes it easily possible to generate faces with subtle differences that globally form a perceptual similarity continuum (Dunsmoor et al., 2011; Onat and Büchel, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on face stimulus generation.

claim: Eight face stimuli were calibrated to span a circular similarity continuum across gender and identity dimensions.
source: eight exploration patterns (colored frames) from a representative individual overlaid on eight face stimuli (1 to 8) calibrated to span a circular similarity continuum across gender and identity dimensions.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the description in the text and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Similarity between the eight faces was calibrated to have a perfect circular organization with lowest dissimilarity between neighbors, and highest dissimilarity for opposing pairs.
source: Similarity between the eight faces was calibrated to have a perfect circular organization with lowest dissimilarity (blue) between neighbors, and highest dissimilarity (yellow) for opposing pairs.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the description and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During the conditioning phase, skin-conductance responses (SCR) were on average 3.8 times higher for CS+ than CS–.
source: During the conditioning phase, skin-conductance responses (SCR) were on average 3.8 times higher for CS+ than CS– (Figure 2B, middle panel bottom row, paired t-test, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expectancy ratings gathered right at the end of the conditioning phase were highest for the CS+ face.
source: In line with this view, expectancy ratings gathered right at the end of the conditioning phase were also highest for the CS+ face (Figure 2B, middle panel top row).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following the conditioning phase the Gaussian model fitted the data significantly better than the flat null model for both SCR and subjective ratings.
source: However, following the conditioning phase the Gaussian model fitted the data significantly better (comparison to flat null model, p<0.001 for SCR and subjective ratings, log-likelihood ratio test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The Gaussian explained both ratings and SCR profiles of single subjects better than the binary function.
source: The Gaussian explained both ratings and SCR profiles of single subjects better than the binary function (AICGauss <AICBin, Ratings: 72/74 and 68/74 subjects in conditioning (median ΔAIC = −3.6) and generalization phase (median ΔAIC = −3.6), SCR: 58/63 subjects in the generalization phase (median ΔAIC = −3.9).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison analysis at the single-subject level.

claim: Before learning, exploration patterns showed an approximately circular similarity structure that followed the physical stimulus similarity structure.
source: Second, before learning, exploration patterns showed an approximately circular similarity structure that followed the physical stimulus similarity structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the FPSA analysis presented in the results section.

claim: After learning the similarity structure changed specifically along the adversity gradient, indicating that CS+ and CS– exploration patterns were modified, while the similarity between other faces remained largely unchanged.
source: Third, after learning the similarity structure changed specifically along the adversity gradient, indicating that CS+ and CS– exploration patterns were modified, while the similarity between other faces remained largely unchanged.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the FPSA analysis presented in the results section.

claim: Participants (n = 74) freely viewed eight faces before and after an aversive learning procedure while eye-movements were measured.
source: Participants (n = 74) freely viewed these faces before and after an aversive learning procedure (Figure 2A) while we measured their eye-movements.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental procedure.

claim: During the conditioning phase, one of the eight faces was introduced as the CS+, being partially reinforced with an aversive outcome (UCS, mild electric shock in ~30% trials).
source: During the conditioning phase, one of the eight faces was introduced as the CS+, being partially reinforced with an aversive outcome (UCS, mild electric shock in ~30% trials).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The CS– was the face most dissimilar to the CS+ (separated by 180°) and was not reinforced.
source: The CS– was the face most dissimilar to the CS+ (separated by 180°) and was not reinforced.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Already during the baseline period the dissimilarity matrix was highly structured.
source: Already during the baseline period the dissimilarity matrix was highly structured (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the FPSA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lowest dissimilarity values (1.05 ± 0.01; M ± SEM) were found between FDMs of neighboring faces.
source: In agreement with a circular similarity geometry and the MDS depiction, lowest dissimilarity values (1.05 ± 0.01; M ± SEM) were found between FDMs of neighboring faces (i.e. first off-diagonal)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FPSA analysis.

claim: FDMs for opposing faces separated by 180° exhibited significantly higher dissimilarity values (1.21 ± 0.01) compared to neighboring faces.
source: whereas FDMs for opposing faces separated by 180° exhibited significantly higher dissimilarity values (1.21 ± 0.01; paired t-test, t(73) = 7.41, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the FPSA analysis with statistical support.

claim: The Perceptual Baseline Model performed significantly better compared to a null model consisting of a constant similarity for all pairwise FDMs comparisons.
source: This model performed significantly better compared to a null model consisting of a constant similarity for all pairwise FDMs comparisons (for Perceptual Model adjusted r2 = 0.09; log-likelihood-ratio test for the alternative null model: p<10−5; BICNullModel = −96.1, BICPerceptual = −244.7; see Supplementary file 1A for the results of model fitting).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: Model parameters at the aggregate level were significantly different from zero for the Perceptual Model in baseline (w Circle = 0.09 ± 0.01, M ± SEM; t(73) = 7.99, p<0.001).
source: Model parameters at the aggregate level were significantly different from zero (Figure 3C; w Circle = 0.09 ± 0.01, M ± SEM; t(73) = 7.99, p<0.001, BICPerceptual = −3.5 ± 1.8, M ± SEM)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Exploration strategies prior to learning mirrored the physical similarity structure of the stimulus set.
source: indicating that exploration strategies prior to learning mirrored the physical similarity structure of the stimulus set.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model fitting results.

claim: Following learning, the circular Perceptual Model performed better compared to the baseline phase (BICPerceptual = −244.7 for the baseline vs. BICPerceptual = −1697.4 for the generalization phase).
source: Following learning, the circular Perceptual Model was again significant (adjusted r2 = 0.35; p<0.001, log-likelihood ratio test), but now performed better compared to the baseline phase (BICPerceptual = −244.7 for the baseline vs. BICPerceptual = −1697.4 for the generalization phase; see Supplementary file 1B for model fitting results).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in the model parameter from baseline to generalization phase (w Circle = 0.13 ± 0.01; paired t-test, t(73) = 4.03, p<0.001).
source: Critically, we found a significant increase in the model parameter from baseline to generalization phase (w Circle = 0.13 ± 0.01; paired t-test, t(73) = 4.03, p<0.001; Figure 3C compare two leftmost bars)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Aversive learning led to a better separation of exploration patterns globally.
source: Overall, these results are compatible with the view that aversive learning led to a better separation of exploration patterns globally, in agreement with the Perceptual Expansion Model (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model fitting results.

claim: The separation between exploration patterns occurred mainly along the adversity gradient defined by the CS+ and CS– faces.
source: However, as already visible in the multi-dimensional scaling method (Figure 3B), the separation between exploration patterns occurred mainly along the adversity gradient defined by the CS+ and CS– faces, whereas the separation along the orthogonal unspecific direction did not exhibit any noticeable changes.
evidence: This is a finding from the MDS visualization and FPSA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Average dissimilarity on the specific dimension increased from 1.21 ± 0.02 in baseline to 1.27 ± 0.02 in the generalization phase (t(73) = 2.54, p<0.05, paired t-test).
source: Regarding individual dissimilarity values, this effect was subtle, with an increase of average dissimilarity on the specific dimension from 1.21 ± 0.02 in baseline to 1.27 ± 0.02 in the generalization phase (t(73) = 2.54, p<0.05, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: Dissimilarity along the orthogonal dimension did not change significantly (1.21 ± 0.03 vs. 1.20 ± 0.02, t(73) = −﻿0.34, p = 0.73, paired t-test).
source: as compared to the orthogonal dimension (1.21 ± 0.03 vs. 1.20 ± 0.02, t(73) = −﻿0.34, p = 0.73, paired t-test,).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: In the generalization phase, dissimilarity along the specific dimension was bigger than along the unspecific dimension (1.27 ± 0.03 vs. 1.20 ± 0.02, t(73) = 2.76, p<0.01, paired t-test).
source: Accordingly, in the generalization phase, dissimilarity along the specific dimension was bigger than along the unspecific dimension (1.27 ± 0.03 vs. 1.20 ± 0.02, t(73) = 2.76, p<0.01, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical support.

claim: The Adversity Gradient Model performed better than the simpler Perceptual Expansion Model (BICPerceptual = −1697.4 vs. BICAdversity. = −1957.5; adjusted r2 = 0.48 vs. 0.35).
source: Model comparison indicated that the more flexible model performed better than the simpler Perceptual Expansion Model (BICPerceptual = −1697.4 vs. BICAdversity. = −1957.5; adjusted r2 = 0.48 vs. 0.35; see Supplementary file 1C–D for fitting results with the Adversity Gradient model on baseline and generalization phases, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: A two-factor repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of experimental phase (F(1, 73) = 6.29, p<0.001).
source: A two-factor (experimental phase ×predictor type) repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of experimental phase (i.e. before vs. after conditioning, F(1, 73) = 6.29, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from ANOVA analysis.

claim: A two-factor repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant interaction of predictor (specific vs. unspecific) with experimental phase F(1,73) = 8.53, p<0.005).
source: as well as a significant interaction of predictor (specific vs. unspecific) with experimental phase F(1,73) = 8.53, p<0.005).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from ANOVA analysis.

claim: The unspecific component did not change from baseline to generalization phase (t(73) = 0.75, p = 0.45).
source: Accordingly, post-hoc analyses showed that while the unspecific component did not change from baseline to generalization phase (t(73) = 0.75, p = 0.45)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post-hoc analysis.

claim: The specific component gained stronger contribution (t(73) = 4.64, p<0.001).
source: the specific component gained stronger contribution (t(73) = 4.64, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post-hoc analysis.

claim: Learning-induced changes were significantly larger in the specific as compared to unspecific component (t(73) = 2.92, p<0.005, paired t-test).
source: and these learning-induced changes were significantly larger in the specific as compared to unspecific component (t(73) = 2.92, p<0.005, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from post-hoc analysis.

claim: 48 subjects out of 74 (65%) showed stronger anisotropy of scanning patterns after learning.
source: 48 subjects out of 74 (65%) showed stronger anisotropy of scanning patterns after learning.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the prevalence of the effect across subjects.

claim: Within the subjects whose shock expectancy ratings indicated successful conditioning (CS+>CS-, nlearner = 61), the prevalence was slightly higher (nanisotropy = 42, i.e. 69%).
source: Next, we studied whether explicit learning of shock contingencies predicted this increase in anisotropy and found that within the subjects whose shock expectancy ratings indicated successful conditioning (CS+>CS-, nlearner = 61), the prevalence was slightly higher (nanisotropy = 42, i.e. 69%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the prevalence of the effect in a subset of subjects.

claim: No Gaussian mixture model of more than one component outperformed the single component model.
source: We found that no Gaussian mixture model of more than one component outperformed the single component model (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the Gaussian mixture model analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The model comparison procedure favored the simpler Adversity Gradient model over the augmented CS+ Attraction Model (BICAdversity. = −1957.5 vs. BICCS+Attraction. = −1923.6 during the generalization phase).
source: The model comparison procedure favored the simpler Adversity Gradient model over the augmented CS+ Attraction Model (BICAdversity. = −1957.5 vs. BICCS+Attraction. = −1923.6 during the generalization phase; adjusted r2 = 0.48; see Supplementary file 1E–F for fitting results with CS+ Attraction Model in baseline and generalization phases, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The parameter estimates for the CS+ centered, Gaussian component were not significantly different from zero neither in baseline or generalization phases.
source: In line with this result, the parameter estimates for the CS+ centered, Gaussian component were not significantly different from zero neither in baseline or generalization phases (wGaussian = −0.009 ± 0.034 in baseline, t(73) = −0.27, p=0.78; wGaussian = 0.02 ± 0.02 in generalization, t(73) = 0.74, p=0.46; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Stronger anisotropy could predict stronger aversive learning, as measured with the modulation depth of fear-tuning profiles coming from subjective ratings (r = 0.25, p=0.03).
source: We found weak, but significant evidence for an association with an increased tuning strength in the ratings (r = 0.25, p=0.03)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis.

claim: The association between anisotropy and tuning strength was only marginally present for SCR (r = 0.23, p=0.07).
source: which was only marginally present for SCR (r = 0.23, p=0.07) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The weights of the unspecific component did not increase when analyzed for separate runs, but if anything showed a trend to decrease with further exposure.
source: However, the weights of the unspecific component did not increase when analyzed for separate runs, but if anything showed a trend to decrease with further exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the run-by-run analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: SVMs were able to decode CS+ vs CS- trials with an accuracy of 56% in the generalization phase compared to 50% in the baseline phase.
source: SVMs were able to decode CS+ vs CS- trials with an accuracy of 56% in the generalization phase compared to 50% in the baseline phase (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SVM classification analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The unspecific direction (−90° vs 90°) could be decoded with an accuracy of 54% during the generalization phase and 52% during the baseline phase.
source: The unspecific direction (−90° vs 90°) could be decoded with an accuracy of 54% during the generalization phase and 52% during the baseline phase.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SVM classification analysis.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant interaction of generalization phase and component (F(72) = 5.4, p=0.02) and a main effect of phase (F(73) = 16.8, p=0.0001).
source: A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant interaction of generalization phase and component (F(72) = 5.4, p=0.02) and a main effect of phase (F(73) = 16.8, p=0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from ANOVA analysis on SVM classification results.

claim: Training SVMs across subjects instead of within subjects did not reproduce the interaction effect (F(73)=0.43, p=0.51).
source: We also tested whether training SVMs across subjects instead of within subjects would reproduce this effect. Here the interaction between generalization phase and component was not significant (F(73)=0.43, p=0.51), suggesting that changes in viewing behavior are idiosyncratic and not necessarily comparable across subjects.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from SVM classification analysis.

claim: Changes in viewing behavior are idiosyncratic and not necessarily comparable across subjects.
source: suggesting that changes in viewing behavior are idiosyncratic and not necessarily comparable across subjects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SVM classification results.

claim: Activation patterns were remarkably different across faces.
source: Qualitatively speaking activation patterns were remarkably different across faces.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the SVM activation patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All activation maps showed subtle changes along the eye region that qualitatively varied with the combination of CS+ and CS- face.
source: In any case, all activation maps showed subtle changes along the eye region that qualitatively varied with the combination of CS+ and CS- face.
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the SVM activation patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The difference in anisotropy reached significance first at the time window corresponding to the interval 400–900 ms after stimulus onset (paired t-test, p=0.03).
source: The difference in anisotropy reached significance first at the time window corresponding to the interval 400–900 ms after stimulus onset (Figure 5A top row, paired t-test, p=0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the temporal FPSA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Adversity-specific exploration started following the first fixation and stayed constant during the stimulus presentation.
source: The same analysis indicated that adversity-specific exploration started following the first fixation (note that the first fixation is the landing fixation on the face following stimulus onset; Figure 5A) and stayed constant during the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a finding from the fixation-rank based temporal FPSA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both before and after learning, specific and unspecific components were strongly localized around the eye region.
source: We found that both before and after learning, specific and unspecific components were strongly localized around the eye region (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the searchlight FPSA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The difference in anisotropy between the baseline and generalization phase was significant only in the eye region (paired t-test uncorrected, p<0.024).
source: We found this interaction to be significant only in the eye region (Figure 5C; paired t-test uncorrected, p<0.024).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the ROI-based FPSA analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The eye region in this study accounted for ~72% of all fixations on the face.
source: Indeed, the eye region in this study accounted for ~72% of all fixations on the face .
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about fixation distribution.

claim: The increased anisotropy during generalization occurred despite a decrease of ~5% in fixation density around the eye region.
source: However, the increased anisotropy during generalization occurred despite a decrease of ~5% in fixation density around the same region (top row in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of fixations, the average saccade distance and entropy showed significant differences between CS+ and CS-, all of which were higher for the CS+.
source: We found that the number of fixations, the average saccade distance and entropy showed significant differences between CS+ and CS-, all of which were higher for the CS+.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of classical eye-movement features.

claim: The only measure exhibiting a significant generalization profile after aversive learning was the saccade length (p<0.001, log-Likelihood Ratio Test of Gaussian against flat null-model).
source: The only measure exhibiting a significant generalization profile, that is bell-shaped tuning curve, after aversive learning was the saccade length (p<0.001, log-Likelihood Ratio Test of Gaussian against flat null-model).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of classical eye-movement features.

claim: None of the classical eye-movement features was able to robustly predict anisotropy (F(4,69) = 0.075, p=0.55, R2adjusted = -0.01).
source: However, none of the features was able to robustly predict anisotropy (F(4,69) = 0.075, p=0.55, R2adjusted = -0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from linear model analysis.

claim: Eyes together with the nose region were the most salient locations across the baseline and generalization phases, and attracted ~91% of all fixation density.
source: In line with previous reports (Walker-Smith et al., 1977), eyes together with the nose region were the most salient locations across the baseline and generalization phases, and attracted ~91% of all fixation density
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about fixation distribution with citation to previous research.

claim: The mouth region had only a marginal contribution with ~3.5% of fixation density.
source: whereas the mouth region had only a marginal contribution with ~3.5%.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about fixation distribution.

claim: Aversive learning increased the number of fixations directed at the nose (+3.6%) and mouth (+0.6%) regions at the expense of the eye region (–5.1%).
source: Investigating changes from baseline to generalization phase, we found that aversive learning increased the number of fixations directed at the nose (+3.6%) and mouth (+0.6%) regions at the expense of the eye region (–5.1%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about changes in fixation distribution.

claim: Model comparison on fixation density favored the flat null model for all regions even at low statistical thresholds in all facial elements across both baseline and generalization phases (p>0.05, log-likelihood test).
source: Most importantly, model comparison on fixation density favored the flat null model for all regions even at low statistical thresholds in all facial elements across both baseline and generalization phases (p>0.05, log-likelihood test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from model comparison on ROI-based fixation counts shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Before aversive learning exploration patterns mirrored the inherent circularity of stimulus similarity.
source: As expected, before aversive learning exploration patterns mirrored the inherent circularity of stimulus similarity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the FPSA analysis.

claim: The exploration of neutral faces in our experimental settings is, at least to some extent, guided by physical characteristics.
source: This is compatible with the view that the exploration of neutral faces in our experimental settings is, at least to some extent, guided by physical characteristics, in contrast to a completely holistic viewing strategy (Peterson and Eckstein, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to previous research.

claim: Aversive learning led to a specific increase in dissimilarity along the direction of the induced adversity gradient.
source: Aversive learning led to a specific increase in dissimilarity along the direction of the induced adversity gradient.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the FPSA analysis.

claim: This adversity-specific exploration strategy appeared early, as soon as the landing fixation, and lasted continuously for the duration of stimulus presentation.
source: This adversity-specific exploration strategy appeared early, as soon as the landing fixation, and lasted continuously for the duration of stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the temporal FPSA analysis.

claim: The finding that fixation strategies change incrementally along the dimension that is predictive of threat offers support for the threat-prediction model.
source: The finding that fixation strategies change incrementally along the dimension that is predictive of threat, in our case captured by the anisotropy of specific vs unspecific components, offers support for the threat-prediction model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical models.

claim: Eye-movement patterns during free-viewing of faces are characterized by strong inter-individual variability.
source: First, eye-movement patterns during free-viewing of faces are characterized by strong inter-individual variability (Coutrot et al., 2016; Kanan et al., 2015; Mehoudar et al., 2014; Walker-Smith et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on eye-movement variability.

claim: Linear classifiers could be trained to predict a volunteer's identity with an average accuracy of ~80% based on fixation maps.
source: This was also true in the present study, where we could train linear classifiers to predict a volunteer's identity with an average accuracy of ~80% based on fixation maps (results not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from additional analysis not shown in the manuscript.

claim: FPSA exploits consistent changes in the similarity relationships of exploration patterns that were defined within-subject.
source: While this inter-individual variability in exploration patterns can dilute the sensitivity of ROI-based approaches, FPSA exploits consistent changes in the similarity relationships of exploration patterns that were defined within-subject.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological advantage of FPSA.

claim: Using multivariate responses allowed to assess changes in similarity between all pairs of stimuli.
source: Second, and equally importantly, using multivariate responses allowed to assess changes in similarity between all pairs of stimuli.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological advantage of FPSA.

claim: On the group-level, the adversity gradient model was found to be most compatible with observed changes in exploration patterns.
source: On the group-level, we found the adversity gradient model to be most compatible with observed changes in exploration patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from model comparison.

claim: Many participants actually did not exhibit the effect of interest on the individual level.
source: While the majority of participants was in line with this view, on the individual level, many participants actually did not exhibit the effect of interest.
evidence: This is an observation about individual differences in the effect.

claim: Anisotropy correlates with indicators of aversive learning as measured by subjective ratings and, to lesser extent with autonomous activity.
source: While we cannot completely exclude a contribution of exposure, we have shown that anisotropy correlates with indicators of aversive learning as measured by subjective ratings and, to lesser extent with autonomous activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis findings.

claim: The unspecific component did not increase with exposure over multiple runs.
source: Furthermore, the unspecific component did not increase with exposure over multiple runs, which would be expected if it was solely driven by exposure.
evidence: This is a summary of the run-by-run analysis findings.

claim: The major drive that leads to the separation of patterns along the specific axis are due to the affective nature of learning, rather than occurring merely as a result of exposure.
source: Therefore, we believe that the major drive that leads to the separation of patterns along the specific axis are due to the affective nature of learning, rather than occurring merely as a result of exposure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings regarding the role of exposure vs. affective learning.

claim: Changes induced by aversive generalization extend beyond autonomous systems or explicit subjective evaluations, but can also affect an entire sensory-motor loop at the systems level.
source: Our results demonstrate that changes induced by aversive generalization extend beyond autonomous systems or explicit subjective evaluations, but can also affect an entire sensory-motor loop at the systems level (Dowd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to previous research.

claim: Participants were 74 naïve healthy males and females (n = 37 each) with normal (or corrected-to-normal) vision (age = 27 ± 4, M ± SD).
source: Participants were 74 naïve healthy males and females (n = 37 each) with normal (or corrected-to-normal) vision (age = 27 ± 4, M ± SD) and without history of psychiatric or neurological diseases, any medical condition or use of medication that would alter pain perception.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: A simple model of the primary visual cortex is known to closely mirror human perceptual similarity judgments.
source: Using a simple model of the primary visual cortex known to closely mirror human perceptual similarity judgments (Yue et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Two dimensions explained a large variance in the MDS analysis of face similarity, while the improvement with the addition of a third dimension was only minor.
source: As expected, while two dimensions explained a large variance, the improvement with the addition of a third dimension was only minor, providing thus evidence that the physical properties of the faces were indeed organized along two-dimensions (stress values for 1D, 2D and 3D resulting from the MDS analysis were 0.42, 0.04, 0.03, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the MDS analysis of face similarity.

claim: The average mean-calibration error across all runs was Mean = 0.36°, Median = 0.34°, SD = 0.11.
source: The average mean-calibration error across all runs was Mean = 0.36°, Median = 0.34°, SD = 0.11.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of eye-tracking calibration quality.
